prompt.raw:
[{"content":"You are extracting a teacher's spoken notes about the children in one class.

The notes arrive as a transcript, in the order the teacher spoke them. The children in this
class are listed below. Names in the transcript are speech-to-text and often misspelt or
mangled; match a spoken name to the listed child it most plausibly is.

Return "observations": the transcript cut into contiguous passages, in order, one passage
per owner, together covering the whole transcript.

Each passage has:
- "kind":
  - "child" — the teacher is talking about one individual child and speaks a name for them.
  - "absent" — the teacher says a named child was not there today ("Théo wasn't in today").
  - "unknown" — the teacher is talking about one individual child but no name is spoken for
    them in this passage or the passage it continues: only a pronoun. Do not guess. The
    teacher will assign it.
  - "group" — a statement about the class as a whole, using a collective referent
    ("everyone", "all the kids", "the class", "they" meaning the whole group). A statement
    that names one child, or describes only one child, is NEVER "group", however it is
    joined to the rest of the sentence.
  - "none" — not an observation about children: the class header, a greeting,
    vocabulary the children are being taught, thinking aloud that describes no child and
    no class.
- "spoken_labels": for a "child" or "absent" passage, the name the teacher speaks for it,
  verbatim as spoken, uncorrected. Empty list for "unknown", "group" and "none".
- "student": for a "child" or "absent" passage, the listed child's name exactly as listed
  below, or "" when no listed child fits. "" for every other kind.
- "summary": the observations in that passage, rewritten as clear sentences.

Rules:
- A child passage runs from where the teacher starts talking about that child to where the
  teacher moves on. It usually opens with the child's name and then continues in pronouns;
  every pronoun sentence after that name belongs to that child until the next child is
  named. Do NOT open a new passage for a pronoun the teacher is still using for the same
  child.
- When the teacher makes the same observation about several named children at once
  ("Zachariah and Anaya did very well", "they both worked well"), return that passage once
  PER CHILD: the same summary repeated, each copy with its own "student". Never fold two
  named children into one passage. This holds when the shared remark opens its own sentence
  after the names: each copy's "spoken_labels" holds the name the teacher spoke for that
  child, never "they" or "both". The shared passage runs from the names to where the teacher
  moves on, pronoun sentences included: after "Maya and Noor did well", a "They did well with
  the colours" belongs to both, so every copy carries the whole of it. The copies differ only
  in "student" and "spoken_labels"; a copy shorter than another is wrong. If the
  observations differ between the children, they are separate passages with different
  summaries. A statement about the class as a whole is still one "group" passage, not one
  per child.
- "student" is set ONLY when the passage's own words, or the passage it continues, speak
  a name for the child — a name that appears in "spoken_labels". A passage that refers to
  the child only by a pronoun ("she", "he") has NO student: it is "unknown", even when
  exactly one listed child has not been mentioned yet. Children on the list who are never
  named were not discussed today. Never assign a passage to a child by
  elimination, by roster order, or because they are the only one left.
- The list of children exists to spell spoken names correctly, not to decide who is
  present.
- The summary uses ONLY the words in its own passage. Never bring in an observation from
  another passage, even an adjacent one.
- The summary keeps the teacher's voice: their vocabulary, their tone, first person if they
  used it. Clean up false starts, filler words and repetitions. Do NOT soften, formalise,
  add or editorialise.
- "none" never takes an observation with it. The header passage ends with the header
  itself: the first sentence that describes the children opens a new passage, even when it
  is spoken in the same breath.

The children in this class:
- Emma
- Ryan
- Lila
","role":"system"},{"content":"Um, so today I wanted to talk about Emma. She, uh, she did great in math today, really got the hang of the multiplication tables we've been working on. And then, let's see... I also wanted to mention Ryan. Ryan was, he was really struggling with the reading comprehension exercise, couldn't quite get the main idea from the passage. Yeah, that's, that's about it for today.","role":"user"}]

  child.

Chloé shows a generally positive attitude toward classroom activities, though her engagement varies. She is willing to participate in group tasks, such as the "Emma is wearing..." activity, and demonstrates cooperation with peers and the teacher. However, she occasionally holds back when new material is introduced, as seen when she repeatedly asked for clarification on tasks she already understood, which required redirection. Her participation improves when working with familiar structures, such as telling her age and gender or repeating story elements, where she contributes more confidently.

BEHAVIOUR

Chloé is integrated within the group but can be easily distracted, particularly when tired or when instructions are being given. She sometimes requires reminders to focus, as noted when she repeatedly asked "quoi quoi quoi" during workshop instructions. Her mood and attentiveness fluctuate; on one occasion, she was in a very good mood and engaged well, while on another, she was noted as distracted and tired. Motivation and Participation

Chloé showed a positive attitude towards the class activities and was open to trying new tasks. She was in a very good mood during one session, and once the traffic light routine was introduced, she participated very well. She especially enjoyed the new story tattoo and the “what’s missing” activity, and she was excited to hear more.

She took part in the different classroom routines and activities, including repeating structures, story time, worksheet work, counting, matching actions to rooms, and using the bingo card. She also joined in practical tasks such as placing tattoos and stickers on the correct body parts, although she sometimes needed a little help. At times, she repeated questions even when she already knew the answer.

Behaviour

Chloé was generally well integrated in the group and responded to reminders from the teacher. The class was a bit loud at the beginning, and she needed to be reminded to listen carefully during workshop instructions. On one occasion she was quite distracted and tired, but she calmed down when reminded. Her repeated questions could become distracting, but she stopped when asked.

Learning

Chloé made progress in the language and structures worked on in class. She could tell her age and gender, almost always using the complete structure, and she could repeat the new vocabulary words and new structures. She also understood and used the “Emma is wearing...” activity, could clean and dress Emma with the correct structure, and understood the clean/dirty and dry/wet concepts. In addition, she could pair up the correct actions with the correct rooms, count very well, and understand the corresponding colour and clothing item on her bingo card.

  • Strengths: she participated well once settled, repeated structures well, understood several classroom activities, and showed good counting skills.
  • Needs support: colours, clothing vocabulary, the story, and using the full structure independently, as well as paying attention during instructions. She also partially understood the numbers songs.
  • Next steps: we will continue practising the vocabulary and structures, especially clothing items and colours, and keep helping her to listen carefully and answer independently.

Mila generally enters the classroom in a happy mood and shows willingness to learn, as seen when she knew vocabulary and repeated structures well. ```html

MOTIVATION AND PARTICIPATION

Mila consistently demonstrates a positive attitude when entering the classroom, often arriving in a very happy mood.

She shows a strong willingness to learn, as evidenced by her ability to recall and repeat vocabulary and structures from previous lessons. For instance, she knew some vocabulary and could repeat the structures during the weather routines.

Mila is generally open to participating in new activities. She enjoys activities like "A present for me," "Dice Game," and "Family Bingo," and actively contributes when she finds them engaging.

Her cooperation with the group and the teacher varies depending on her mood. While she can become upset when things do not go her way, she typically calms down and re-engages with the activities. For example, she initially closed up when she did not get her way but improved as the class progressed.

Mila's participation is notable when she is interested in the activity. She actively contributes to group tasks, such as helping to hand out materials, and participates enthusiastically in action activities. Her ability to tell stories with minimal help, such as recounting parts of the story with almost no assistance, highlights her engagement when she feels confident.

However, she may hold back when faced with new or challenging material. For instance, she needed help with specific words during the weather routines and initially did not participate in routines when she struggled with a stamp activity. Continued practice and support will help her feel more comfortable with new challenges.

BEHAVIOUR

Mila is generally integrated within the group, though she can become easily frustrated in certain situations. For example, she laid down, was asked to sit, and turned her back during story time due to anger when she could not see the Big Book.

Her behaviour often reflects her mood and the group's dynamics. On days when the class seemed to get bored by the end of the story, her participation also waned. However, she can overcome initial reluctance; when she said she had a headache, she still participated in the activities.

Specific situations, such as not being allowed to keep blu-tack, led to her refusing to participate in certain activities like the True or False activity and the Dice Game. These instances suggest that her behaviour is closely tied to her emotional state and sense of fairness.

LEARNING

Mila has shown a strong grasp of the structures and vocabulary worked on during the story. She could repeat structures well and use new vocabulary words effectively during activities.

Her level of learning objectives achieved is commendable. She could tell the story with almost no help and combined moods and actions very well. Additionally, she knew the phrases associated with her weather card and could perform weather and clothing item combinations effectively.

Strengths:

  • Strong recall of vocabulary and structures from previous lessons
  • Ability to tell stories with minimal assistance
  • Effective combination of moods and actions during activities
  • Enthusiastic participation in activities she enjoys

Weaknesses and Plan for Improvement:

  • Occasionally struggles with specific words or routines, such as "taking off" and "putting on" during weather routines. Continued practice in context will build confidence and familiarity.
  • May become frustrated when unable to complete tasks immediately, leading to temporary withdrawal. We will work on emotional regulation strategies and emphasize that mistakes are part of learning.

The school is committed to supporting Mila in these areas by providing additional practice opportunities and encouraging a positive and resilient attitude toward learning.

At times, Mila held back when she did not get her way or when an activity was less familiar. On some occasions she only listened at first, did not join the routines straight away, or refused to take part in activities such as True or False and the Dice Game. On one day she said she had a headache, but she did take part in the activities afterwards.

Overall, Mila’s behaviour was often very good, and on several days it was described as relatively great. She participated well with the group, although her mood sometimes affected how she behaved. When she became upset, she could close up, lie down a few times, be asked to sit, and turn her back during story time. She was also upset when she could not see the Big Book and did not move to get a better view.

The class needed a lot of movement and seemed to get bored by the end of the story, so a varied pace continues to be helpful for Mila.

Learning

Mila achieved many of the learning objectives worked on in class. She could use the new vocabulary words during activities, repeat the structures very well, and knew the phrase that went with her weather card. She also knew the story well enough to tell it with almost no help, or to tell part of it and repeat the rest. In addition, she combined the mood and actions very well, matched the weather and clothing item combinations very well, completed the worksheet activity very well, and showed that she knew the colour vocabulary, including white and black.

Camille participates well when she feels comfortable, and she shows interest in the language being worked on, especially when she can recall vocabulary and repeat what she has learned. At times she can be a little more hesitant, but with encouragement she responds well and continues to engage positively with the group.

Learning process

Assessment (Learning process): Good

Comment:
Camille has shown a good understanding of the story and the language structures worked on this term. She can remember vocabulary words very well, especially colours, clothing items and some prepositions, and she also demonstrated understanding in activities about what Oliver and Baby could or could not do. She was able to recite parts of the story and to repeat when asked, showing that she is memorising the language and building her confidence. She sometimes needs help to recall the correct structures, particularly when asking questions or using the new language independently, but she shows real understanding and is making steady progress. Continued practice will help her become more secure and more confident when using the structures spontaneously.

Behaviour

Assessment (Behaviour): Very good

Comment:
Camille has a peaceful, easy-going and attentive manner in class. She is generally well integrated within the group and her calm presence helps create a positive atmosphere. She is usually focused and listens carefully, showing a good level of concentration during activities. On occasion she can be a little playful with the materials or slightly distracted with a classmate, but this does not affect her overall behaviour, which remains very good. Camille responds well to guidance, follows the classroom routine and shows a kind and cooperative attitude towards both the teacher and her peers.

Marks

Oral Test Mark: 8.10  Good. Camille can understand the question and answers either with a single word or with a structure which is only partially correct.

Final comment

____________________________________________________________
Camille has had a positive term and has shown good understanding of the story content and vocabulary worked on in class. Her calm and attentive nature, together with her willingness to participate, have contributed well to the group. She is progressing nicely and, with continued practice and confidence, she will keep developing her language skills next term.

Motivation and Participation

Camille was attentive overall and very attentive. She was happy to listen to the story and seemed to really enjoy the new story. She loved the Present for me activity and the Who's missing activity. She also understood the worksheet activity and could do the worksheet about what Oliver and Baby could or couldn't do very well. She knew parts of the story, could recite the story partially, and could repeat when asked to repeat. She needed help to remember the correct structures for a lot of the activities, but she showed a real understanding and a certain memorisation of the vocabulary.

Behaviour

Camille was a bit distracting with Zoé, but it was alright. She was not always giving the material back directly when asked and was hiding it jokingly. The group was bored by the end of the story. Camille was a bit less confident today and seemed more hesitant, but she was encouraged and seemed quite happy.

Learning

  • Camille remembered the vocabulary words very well, including the colours and clothing items, and she could remember some prepositions.
  • She quickly understood the new weather and action miming routine, as well as the new mood routine with "he's smiling because he's happy."
  • She understood the worksheet activity about what Oliver and Baby could or couldn't do very well.
  • She is still learning to ask questions about the person's physical appearance before just asking who it is; this is a work in progress.
  • Her strengths are her good memory for vocabulary and her quick understanding of new routines and activities.
  • Her main weakness at the moment is the question structure, and support will continue with this area.
